items.item: A dead tuple is the old heap tuple version MVCC's own append-only design leaves behind after an UPDATE or DELETE; VACUUM's standard form marks that space reusable but does not return it to the operating system except at the very end of the file.

at.step: Reveal: a dead tuple, counted directly

items.item: HOT (heap-only tuple) updates skip creating new index entries and can opportunistically prune now-invisible intermediate row versions outside of VACUUM entirely, but only when the update touches no indexed column and the page has enough free space left — exactly the condition this chapter's previous topic's own growth experiment had to defeat by indexing the updated column.

at.step: Reveal: HOT updates, the free optimization

items.item: The visibility map records which pages are known all-visible so vacuum can skip them on the next run and so an index-only scan can skip fetching the heap tuple entirely; it exists specifically because Postgres's own indexes carry no visibility information of their own.

at.step: Reveal: HOT updates, the free optimization

items.item: Autovacuum decides whether to vacuum a table from a threshold formula — the minimum of a configured maximum and a base threshold plus a scale factor times the table's row count — not from a fixed schedule, and ordinary autovacuum workers yield to a conflicting lock, but one running specifically to prevent wraparound does not.

A long-running open transaction pins Postgres's xmin horizon: as long as it holds a snapshot, VACUUM cannot treat any row that snapshot could still see as dead-and-reclaimable, so every table the transaction could read grows for as long as it stays open — found in practice via pg_stat_activity's own backend_xmin age.

at.step: Reveal: the xmin horizon, held open

items.item: A stale prepared transaction (two-phase commit left uncommitted) pins the horizon the identical way an ordinary long transaction does, found via pg_prepared_xacts, and must be explicitly committed or rolled back — Postgres has no timeout that cleans one up on its own.

at.step: Reveal: the xmin horizon, held open

items.item: An abandoned replication slot pins the horizon even once its standby is disconnected or gone entirely: a slot holds back not just the WAL segments a standby hasn't received yet, but also the specific rows vacuum would otherwise be free to remove — found via pg_replication_slots' own xmin and catalog_xmin.

at.step: Reveal: the xmin horizon, held open

items.item: A real transaction held open against this sandbox's own cluster while a concurrent workload updates the same table makes the pin's cost visible directly: table size (and dead-tuple count) grows for as long as the transaction stays open, then drops once it is released and autovacuum actually runs.

Postgres compares 32-bit transaction IDs with circular (modulo-2^32) arithmetic, not simple greater-than; VACUUM's freezing marks a row's insert XID as permanently 'in the past' via the special FrozenTransactionId value, so a row can survive the counter wrapping around without ever appearing to be from the future.

at.step: Reveal: freezing and the wraparound shutdown

items.item: Postgres gives explicit, escalating warning before the failure: a warning once a database's oldest XIDs are forty million transactions from wraparound, then an outright refusal to assign any new write-transaction XID once fewer than three million remain — read-only transactions can still start, but every write fails.

at.step: Reveal: freezing and the wraparound shutdown

items.item: Sentry's own 2015 production outage is a real instance of exactly this failure: a write-heavy, large-table workload hit the wraparound protection and went fully write-blocked for most of a working day, caused by autovacuum_freeze_max_age tuned too high and too much cost delay — and 'just disable autovacuum,' which Sentry's own postmortem calls out as common bad advice, is the precise opposite of the fix.

at.step: Reveal: freezing and the wraparound shutdown

items.item: Postgres's own documented recovery procedure, once wraparound protection has tripped, is not 'restart in single-user mode': resolve old prepared transactions, end long-running open transactions, drop stale replication slots, then run VACUUM on the target database — and never VACUUM FULL in that state, since it itself requires a fresh XID.

Multixact IDs — the separate 32-bit counter and wraparound mechanism for row-level locks held by more than one transaction at once — share the same freeze/wraparound shape as ordinary XIDs but are a distinct mechanism with their own thresholds.

at.out: a distinct counter and wraparound path from ordinary XID wraparound; teaching both in one 15-minute topic would blur the mechanism this topic is actually about
